*   MPs Dr. Melkote and Sangam Lakshmibayamma prepared to resign their Lok Sabha seats in protest of these arrests.

### 26–27 June — The Chief Minister's "Resignation Drama"

*   On 26 June, lawyers in the twin cities staged a 400-car rally to Raj Bhavan, submitting a memorandum demanding dismissal of the state government and imposition of President's Rule; students and teachers separately protested demanding ministers' resignations, and Brooke Bond industry workers joined a strike for the first time, protesting the arrest of Telangana leaders.
*   Telangana ministers, under pressure from agitators, decided to resign en masse, planning to submit resignations to the Governor on the evening of 27 June — but Industrial Minister Guru Murthy pre-emptively submitted his resignation directly to the Chief Minister instead.
*   Realizing that a mass ministerial resignation would strengthen the movement and threaten his own position, Chief Minister Brahmananda Reddy staged what amounted to a political drama: he sent his own resignation letter on 27 June not to the Governor, but to Congress President Nijalingappa in Delhi — a technicality that rendered it a non-genuine resignation, since a resignation must go to the Governor to be effective.
*   With the Chief Minister's own resignation thus rendered non-binding, Telangana ministers were left in a difficult position; nonetheless, **eight Telangana ministers** did resign to support the movement: J.V. Narsinga Rao, Sheelam Siddha Reddy, PV Narasimha Rao, Arige Ramaswami, VB Raju, BV Gurumurthy, KV Narayana Reddy, and Ibrahim Ali Ansari.
*   The Governor accepted these eight ministers' resignations on 14 July, but Brahmananda Reddy's resignation was rejected by the party high command, as he had expected.
*   As part of a plan between Brahmananda Reddy and Nijalingappa, the matter of the Chief Minister's resignation was left to the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, which met on 6 July under Nijalingappa and Kamaraj.
*   Minister PV Narasimha Rao moved a resolution expressing complete confidence in the Chief Minister, which the legislature unanimously approved; state Congress legislators separately declared confidence in Brahmananda Reddy.
*   Notably, this "unanimous" confidence vote occurred while 9 Telangana MLAs and several Legislative Council members were in jail and remaining Telangana members were absent — undermining the vote's representativeness of Telangana opinion.

### 1 July

*   Nearly a thousand auto- and taxi-drivers in Telangana held a procession and submitted a petition to the Governor, followed by a public meeting at Khairatabad railway station grounds expressing full support for the movement.

### 2–7 July — Continued Arrests Under the PD Act

*   On 2 July, student leader PJ Suri was arrested in Secunderabad; Mallikarjuna was arrested on 3 July under the PD Act and sent to Rajahmundry jail. All those detained under the PD Act filed writs in the High Court seeking release.
*   The same day, the Congress Working Committee, meeting in Delhi, decided against a separate Telangana.
*   **4 July**: TPS treasurer Ramakrishna Dooth was arrested under the PD Act along with Dr. Gopal Kishan (Assistant Surgeon, Osmania Hospital, and president of the Andhra Pradesh Medical Students Association) and four others; Dr. Gopal Kishan is noted as the **first Gazetted Officer arrested under the PD Act anywhere in India**.
*   **People gheraoed Minister VB Raju** on 4 July, demanding he accept a separate Telangana and holding a strike at his office for hours, forcing him to sit on the floor with them; the satyagraha was led by pharmaceutical-company owner Gupta.
*   5 July was observed as **Telangana Liberation Day**.
*   A separate-Andhra conference was held in Guntur on 5 July, chaired by Nadimpally Narsimha Rao; Independent Party leader N. Vijayaraj Kumar argued the Gentlemen's Agreement had gone unimplemented for 13 years and that bifurcation into two states would benefit both regions' development. Telangana leaders Sadalakshmi and Sridhar Reddy sent messages of support to this conference.
*   Congress President Nijalingappa's 6 July visit to Hyderabad was met with an absolute bandh; police fired at Khairatabad.
*   Addressing a Calcutta meeting, Jayaprakash Narayan said Telangana had been neglected, and that forming smaller states would not endanger national unity.
*   On 7 July, activists bombed the house of Deputy Chief Minister J.V. Narsinga Rao (an advocate for Vishalandhra) in protest; the same day, high-school girls surrounded Nijalingappa at his Hyderabad guesthouse, chanting slogans for separate Telangana.

### 8–12 July

*   On 8 July, Revenue Minister VB Raju told reporters the people of Telangana were discontented and disappointed, and urged Andhra people to hand over the state's leadership to Telangana.
*   **10 July — Telangana Protections Day** and **Black Flag Day** were observed. At the AICC meeting in Bangalore, MP J. Rameshwar Rao proposed a Congress-regulation amendment aimed at forming a separate Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee.
*   On 11 July, the AICC meeting in Bangalore did not discuss the separate-state issue at all, disappointing Telangana supporters; police lathi-charged striking employee families in Abids the same day.
*   **12 July — Telangana Liberation Day** (again observed) and **Telangana Flag Day**: the TPS organized Flag Day across Telangana; police arrested MP GS Melkote for unfurling a separate-Telangana flag at Isamia Bazaar; a motor-vehicle procession displayed a flag depicting Telangana's territory, and Telangana flags were hoisted on schools, government offices, and even the Charminar.

### 16 July — TNGO Withdraws Its Strike

*   The TNGO called off its indefinite strike (running since 10 June, for 37 days); employees returned to duty, and all temporary employees hired during the strike were dismissed.
*   Amos resigned from the TNGO due to internal differences of opinion.

**Reasons for the strike's withdrawal:**

*   The government lured a few employee leaders, causing splits within the TNGO.
*   While prominent employee leaders were in jail, Chief Minister Brahmananda Reddy negotiated a deal with INTUC president G. Sanjeevareddy, sowing disturbances within the NGO and prompting the strike's withdrawal.
*   AP State Union Congress General Secretary N. Sathyanarayana Reddy criticized the movement, alleging the Birla business group was backing it to further its own interests over Alwin Metals in Hyderabad — though this claim of Birla financial backing was never confirmed.
*   Osmania University employees also called off their strike on 23 July.

### 18 July — New Cabinet

*   Kasu Brahmananda Reddy rebuilt his cabinet on 18 July after the Governor formally accepted the eight Telangana ministers' resignations.
*   J.V. Narsinga Rao was appointed Deputy Chief Minister, and Jalagam Vengal Rao (from Andhra) became Home Minister.
*   Speaking in Palvancha on 5 August, Vengal Rao vowed to suppress the movement as Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel had suppressed the Razakars.
*   Roda Mistri, Vasudeva Rao, V. Purushottam Reddy, and G. Sangeeva Reddy were also newly inducted as ministers from Telangana.

### 19 July — Anti-Traitor's Day

*   The TPS and Student Action Committee organized a Telangana Bandh to protest the Telangana ministers who joined the reconstituted cabinet, observed as "Anti-Traitor's Day."

### 24–25 July — Parliamentary Committee Push and Private Bill

*   On 24 July, Telangana MP M. Narayana Reddy wrote to the Lok Sabha Speaker proposing a 21-member Parliamentary Committee to study the Telangana issue and report by 26 August, 1969; the letter was signed by more than 40 MPs across states, including Vajpayee.
*   The **Telangana Regional Committee** formed a 22-member subcommittee to suggest a solution, with TPS president Chokka Rao appointing ministers and legislators from various parties as members.
*   On 25 July, Independent MP Narayana Reddy introduced a private bill in the Lok Sabha proposing a referendum on Telangana's future; this bill was debated on 21 August, 1969.

### 1–2 August

*   On 1 August, a TPS conference at Khammam, chaired by Kandibanda Rama Rao, saw acting president T.N. Sada Lakshmi vow to fight for a separate state "till death."
*   On 2 August, Sridhar Reddy (President, Rebel TPS) and 10 student leaders were arrested under the PD Act — after he had announced on 31 July that an indefinite Telangana bandh would begin 11 August, along with a boycott of Independence Day.

### 5–10 August — Firings and Satyagraha

*   **5 August**: at Home Minister Jalagam Vengal Rao's congratulatory meeting in Kothagudem, police fired on protesters, killing students Dastagiri (10) and Ram Chander (25).
*   **6 August**: under P. Vasudev's (President, Store Clerks' Association) leadership, clerks staged satyagraha on President's Road, Secunderabad, and were arrested; separately, young man Chepalabavi Rabindranath was killed in police firing at Rajeshwara Talkies market area, Secunderabad, and Mahadev Singh was arrested there the same day.
*   Union Home Minister Y.B. Chavan, speaking in the Rajya Sabha, said the Union government was not favourably disposed toward forming a separate state.
*   **7 August**: State Home Minister Vengal Rao alleged Naxalites were infiltrating the movement and causing violence, claiming 90% of people wanted a united state.
*   **8 August**: former minister V.B. Raju proposed a Triple Point Scheme — a change in government leadership, release of all political prisoners, and a round-table conference of Telangana leaders.
*   **9 August**: Sarvodaya activists, under leader Ghora, met in Hyderabad to plan awareness-building efforts about the movement in non-Telangana areas and among Andhra people.
*   **10 August**: Kaloji Narayana Rao and Warangal medical student leader Kolluri Chiranjeevi were arrested under Section 151 for satyagraha in Warangal.

### 14–16 August

*   Three legislators — J. Eshwaribai, Palwai Govardhan Reddy, and DV Sudhakar — were arrested under the PD Act on 14 August.
*   At the AP Legislative Council on 14 August, Governor Khandubhai Khasamji Desai's inaugural address was interrupted by "Jai Telangana" slogans, forcing him to return without completing his speech; Student Working Committee president Gottam Gopala Reddy was arrested during this protest.
*   **15 August**: a large meeting under TPS auspices at Vivekavardhini College — addressed by Sadalakshmi, Sumitradevi, and Konda Venkata Rangareddy — hoisted the National Flag alongside the Telangana Flag on Independence Day. Police lathi-charged students afterward; Sada Lakshmi was injured by a tear-gas shell, and legislator Sumitra Devi was wounded, later displaying her blood-stained clothes publicly in protest. K. Rajamallu raised the issue of the lathi-charge on Sumithra Devi in the Assembly.
*   **16 August**: the AP Legislative Assembly observed two minutes' silence for those killed since January 1969; Deputy CM JV Narsingarao moved the resolution, with BV Subba Reddy as Speaker.

**President's election and its effect on Telangana:**

*   The Presidential election (held 16 August, 1969) became another distraction that allowed the high command to overlook Brahmananda Reddy's handling of the crisis.
*   Following President Zakir Hussain's death, Congress President Nijalingappa and PM Indira Gandhi disagreed over the party's presidential candidate — Nijalingappa backed Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy, while Indira Gandhi backed VV Giri.
*   Indira Gandhi tried to keep Brahmananda Reddy on her side ahead of the election, given his following in Andhra Pradesh, but he ultimately declared support for Nijalingappa's candidate, Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy.
*   Legislators and MPs seeking a separate Telangana voted instead for VV Giri (Indira Gandhi's candidate), who went on to win the election.

### 18 August — Lok Sabha and Assembly Debates

*   Jana Sangh member KL Gupta proposed a Lok Sabha resolution urging central action on Telangana.
*   MPs G. Venkataswamy and Dr. Melkote urged the Centre to intervene, dissolve the state government, and impose President's Rule; Dr. Melkote stated that 250 activists had been killed over the preceding eight months and nearly 50,000 arrested, displaying photographs of martyrs and vowing continued struggle.
*   People's Socialist Party leader S.N. Dvivedi compared the Telangana unrest to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
*   Independent MP N.G. Ranga said the agitation had broad popular support and urged the Centre to quickly decide whether Telangana should be a sub-state or a fully separate state.
*   S.V. Krishnappa proposed setting up a States Reorganization Committee to examine backward-area problems nationally.
*   DMK's N.K. Dappan argued the movement showed that shared language alone did not guarantee unity.
*   Communist Party member Yogendra Sharma warned his party would also push for separate states for other backward regions if the Centre failed to address regional disparities.
*   In the AP Legislative Assembly, Congress member P. Narsa Reddy proposed a resolution thanking the Governor's speech while urging release of detained leaders to enable a round-table meeting, and calling on activists to halt their agitation; independent Andhra legislator Chappidi Vengaiah said the preceding seven months had shown there was no option but a separate Telangana state.

### 21–30 August

*   **21 August**: the Chief Minister announced a Rs 60-crore fertilizer plant at Ramagundam, seen as an attempt to subdue the movement.
*   The TNGO Association and State Teachers' Association — dissolved by the government on 24 May — were revived on 21 August.
*   **22 August**: Home Minister Y.B. Chavan rejected the proposal for a Parliamentary Committee on Telangana, prompting eight Lok Sabha MPs (seven Telangana Congress MPs — G.S. Melkote, Baker Ali Mirja, J. Rameshwar Rao, G. Venkataswamy, P. Gangareddy, Ramapati Rao, R. Surender Reddy — plus Mysore's M.V. Krishnappa) to walk out of the House.
*   **23 August**: wives of movement leaders (Mrs. Chenna Reddy, Mrs. Achyuta Reddy, Mrs. Narottam Reddy, and others) met the Prime Minister demanding intervention; she said she would not intervene until the movement ceased and peace prevailed.
*   **24 August**: 23 detenus held under the PD Act at Chanchalguda and Rajahmundry jails, including TPS treasurer Ramakrishna Dhooth and Student Action Committee leader Gopal, were released on the Advisory Committee's recommendation.
*   **25 August**: an AP High Court division bench ordered the release of Marri Chenna Reddy, Konda Laxman Bapuji, and all 34 detenus; they were released in Delhi on 27 August.
*   **26 August**: a six-member delegation of the Telangana Workers Party met President VV Giri to press for intervention.
*   **27 August**: Konda Laxman Bapuji and Marri Chenna Reddy met Congress President Nijalingappa and PM Indira Gandhi in Delhi. Bapuji separately met the Home Minister and Deputy PM Morarji Desai, while Chenna Reddy met President VV Giri, both seeking an early resolution. Chenna Reddy also addressed a meeting of Telangana MPs in Delhi, blaming 13 years of injustice for the current movement, and urged them to work toward a Parliamentary Committee.
*   **28 August**: Lakshminarayana was elected Mayor of Hyderabad, backed by the TPS — a further morale boost for the movement.
*   **29 August**: Chenna Reddy and Konda Laxman returned from Delhi to a warm welcome in Hyderabad.
*   **30 August**: at a Reddy Hostel meeting chaired by Sadalakshmi, Chenna Reddy and Mallikarjun vowed not to stop the movement until statehood was achieved — but from September onward, the movement entered a **declining phase**.

### 1–4 September

*   Detainees J. Eshwari Bai, G.V. Sudhakar, and Palwai Govardhan Reddy (held since 14 August) were released on 1 September; Sridhar Reddy, president of the Rebel Praja Samiti, was released on 3 September.
*   On 4 September, Neelam Sanjeeva Reddy suggested a second State Reorganisation Committee, a proposal Congress President Nijalingappa rejected.

### 5 September — Teachers' Misery Day

*   Teachers observed "Teachers Miserable Day," wearing black badges and holding meetings demanding implementation of the Kothari Committee recommendations.
*   Education Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, speaking in the Assembly the same day, accused politicians of using students for the ongoing movement; 12 Telangana Congress members walked out in protest.

### 6 September — Meetings on Resolution

*   Government Chief Whip Parigi Ram Reddy — a longtime Brahmananda Reddy loyalist — held a meeting of 52 legislators and ministers on steps to resolve the Telangana issue; Telangana activists were absent.
*   Minister VB Raju separately convened an all-party meeting at the Exhibition Grounds, attended by both Telangana-statehood supporters and others.

### 16–30 September — Internal Splits Deepen

*   On 16 September, at Vivekavardhini College, Mallikarjun warned that Telangana people would form a "rebel government" if statehood demands were not met.
*   TPS president Marri Chenna Reddy launched the _Jai Telangana Weekly_ magazine in Hyderabad on 17 September, published under Sangamreddy Satyanarayana's auspices.
*   On 18 September, Warangal Medical Students' leader K. Chiranjeevi urged students to temporarily suspend the movement, resume classes, and not lose the academic year.
*   On 22 September, Chenna Reddy and Konda Laxman Bapuji met President VV Giri at Bollaram to discuss Telangana.
*   On 23 September, the TPS and Student Action Committee — signed by Chenna Reddy and Mallikarjun — announced students should return to classes immediately; Reddy informed President Giri of this decision, and the President expressed his approval.
*   This decision provoked further internal dissent: Rebel TPS vice-president Veerareddy accused Chenna Reddy of betraying the movement from within; Captain Ansari (TPS leader) criticized the Congress party for turning the movement into an internal party struggle; and Rebel TPS president Sridhar Reddy insisted the decision belonged to students alone, not to Chenna Reddy or Mallikarjun.
*   Hyderabad old-city students began a relay hunger strike at Charkaman, criticizing the class-attendance decision and demanding Telangana leaders resign; leaders of this protest included Swayam Prakash, Tamizoddin Ahmad, K. Govind, and Mohammad Aliuddin Khureshi.
*   On 25 September, Assembly Speaker B.V. Subbareddy moved a no-confidence motion, backed by 11 legislators demanding a separate Telangana.
*   On 27 September, Education Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao announced in the Assembly that 120 non-mulki teachers had been removed from Telangana and would be reappointed in Andhra.
*   On 28 September, a separate-Telangana meeting at Kothagudem, chaired by Kamal Mustafa Khan, was addressed by Marri Chenna Reddy, Ananthula Madan Mohan, and T. Hayagriva Chari.

### 10–18 October — Renewed Satyagraha and Fasts

*   **10 October**: with students criticized for resuming classes, Chenna Reddy announced he would undertake satyagraha alongside adult (18+) participants from this date; on the first day, three lakh people joined the satyagraha at his invitation.
*   The same day, Mallikarjun launched an indefinite fast at the Gandhi Statue in Secunderabad, protesting the Centre's continued inaction on Telangana statehood.
*   On 18 October, fifteen-year-old Kumari Ramadevi (Convener, Telangana Students' — girls' — Action Committee) began an indefinite fast at the Raja Bahadur Venkatarama Reddy statue near Narayanaguda YMCA circle.
*   Mallikarjun's fast was ended by police arrest and hospitalization on 3 November, after 24 days.
*   On 11 October, Swatantra Party member Gauthu Lachanna announced support for dividing the state under the slogan "Andhra for the Andhras," arguing separation would let coastal Andhra develop and increase revenue.
*   On 12 October, a Youth Congress meeting at Chikkadpally, chaired by G. Venkatswamy, saw Konda Laxman Bapuji inaugurate the "Telangana Pradesh Youth Congress Committee" branch.
*   On 13 October, activists bombed the houses of State Social Welfare Minister Roda Mistri and Home Minister Jalagam Vengala Rao.
*   On 14 October, MP Mir Akbar Alikhan proposed: (1) granting the Telangana Regional Council extensive powers via presidential order, and (2) a round-table conference chaired by the PM or Home Minister to discuss the presidential order before a constitutional amendment.

### 23–31 October

*   **23 October**: K. Narasimhareddy (President, Telangana Liberation Committee, Warangal) launched a tax-refusal movement, run in the spirit of the national freedom movement, in Warangal district.
*   **24 October**: Jalil Pasha and Vishnuvardhan Reddy began a fast at the Nehru statue, Abids.
*   **31 October**: bombs were thrown at the houses of Telangana ministers Rhoda Mistry and Jalagam Vengal Rao.

### 1–27 November — Winding Down

*   **1 November**: Konda Laxman Bapuji began an 11-day fast at his residence, Jaladrushyam, timed to the anniversary of Andhra Pradesh's formation, to highlight the "breach of contract" to Telangana; his daughter Sumitra persuaded him to end it on 12 November with fruit juice.
*   The TPS declared 1 November "Anti-Andhra Pradesh Day," organizing relay hunger strikes; the Telangana Fourth Class Employees' Association called it "Candidates Day."
*   Bakar Ali Mirza resigned from Congress in November 1969 in protest of both state and central governments' handling of Telangana.
*   **27 November**: returning from Delhi, Chenna Reddy announced the movement would be postponed and revived from 1 January of the following year — effectively ending the year-long active phase of the movement.

### 5–29 December — Factional Struggle Within TPS

*   **5 December**: former president Sadalakshmi, with three others, issued a statement removing Chenna Reddy from the TPS presidency, criticizing his introduction of a "person worship" method and dominating attitude.
*   **26 December**: at a TPS meeting, Chenna Reddy was unanimously re-elected president.
*   **29 December**: Mallikarjun was unanimously elected head of the Student United Action Committee.

concepts.bodyMd:
*   _Janadharma_, a Warangal weekly edited and owned by Sri Madabhushi Srinivasacharya, was distinctive in publicly and consistently defending the movement, reporting events as they actually occurred.
*   Alongside _Janadharma_, the _Andhra Bhoomi_ and _Deccan Chronicle_ also published some news favourable to the movement.
*   In contrast, _Andhra Magazine_, _Vishalandhra Magazine_, and _Andhra Jyoti Magazine_ opposed the separate-Telangana movement and its leaders, publishing false and misleading reports about it.

concepts.partName: The Role of Various Parties in the Movement
concepts.bodyMd:
### Congress Party

*   Leaders such as Konda Laxman Bapuji initially demanded autonomous status, not full statehood, for Telangana.
*   In April 1969, eight Telangana Congress MLAs declared a separate state the only solution — but after the Eight-Point Formula's announcement on 11 April, **48 Telangana Congress MLAs** issued a joint statement instead demanding immediate implementation of the formula, saying a separate state was unnecessary. This division within Congress persisted throughout the year.
*   Protesters responded to this stance by stoning Labour Minister K.V. Narayan Reddy's car at Khairatabad, and unidentified persons later bombed the houses of Minister G. Sanjeeva Reddy and Transport Minister Lakshminarasayya.
*   On 19 September, 1969, 70 Telangana MLAs appealed to the Centre to change the state's leadership.
*   On 15 December, 1969, 82 of the 135 AP Congress Committee members from Telangana (including Deputy CM J.V. Narsinga Rao) notified the PM that Telangana did not need a separate Pradesh Congress Committee — leading the PM to conclude the majority of Congress leaders opposed dividing the state.
*   On 16 December, 1969, however, 90 pro-Chief-Minister Telangana Congress leaders took a unanimous decision favouring the Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee.
*   **Cause → Effect**: this back-and-forth illustrates that Telangana Congress leaders lacked unity throughout the movement, weakening the political case for statehood even as popular agitation continued.

### CPM

*   Opposed a separate Telangana, giving the slogan _"Vishalandhra lo Praja Rajyam"_ ("People's rule within a united Andhra"), while still demanding effective implementation of Telangana's existing safeguards.

### CPI

*   Also favoured a united state, while demanding implementation of Telangana protections.
*   The party and its subsidiaries (AITUC, AISF, AIYF) demanded the government's dismissal and the imposition of President's Rule.
*   Rajabahadur Gaur (Hyderabad) and Dasari Nagabhushanam (Vijayawada) undertook hunger strikes to press for the government's ouster and President's Rule.
*   CPI leader Magdum Moinuddin, in internal party discussions, urged the party to press for the legality of the Telangana Regional Committee and a Telangana Public Service Commission.

### Jana Sangh

*   Opposed formation of a separate Telangana state as a matter of party policy.
*   Hyderabad City Secretary C.M. Jaganmohan Reddy nonetheless defended the movement publicly and was expelled from the party as a result.
*   In the Lok Sabha, Jana Sangh member Chand Goyal argued that both central and state governments were trying to make Telangana a "permanent backward state."

### Swatantra Party

*   Gave its complete support to a separate Telangana, and — as noted earlier — was the first political party to formally demand it.

### United Socialist Party (USP)

*   At Indira Gandhi's April 1969 meeting with opposition leaders, the USP proposed making Telangana a sub-state within Andhra Pradesh, rather than a fully separate state.

### Praja Socialist Party (PSP)

*   On 2 April, 1969, issued a resolution demanding the Brahmananda Reddy government's dissolution and imposition of President's Rule.

### Praja Party

*   On 25 September, 1969, the party's working committee in Vijayawada stated that delays in resolving the Telangana issue had deepened Telangana people's distrust of the Centre, and called for implementing the recommendations of the various committees formed so far.

concepts.partName: Reasons for the Failure of the 1969 Movement
concepts.bodyMd:
*   The movement began among students, teachers, employees, and intellectuals, but as it escalated, opportunist politicians took over its leadership.
*   **Cause → Effect**: this shift turned the movement into a Congress Party affair, and ultimately into an internal struggle within the Congress Party itself, diluting its original mass character.
*   Leadership fractured into three rival groups:
    1.  Telangana Praja Samithi, under Marri Chenna Reddy
    2.  Telangana Congress Committee, under Konda Laxman Bapuji
    3.  Telangana United Front, under VB Raju and Narottama Reddy
*   Only 24 of 74 Telangana Congress MLAs fully backed the movement; even these dissenters opposed Kasu Brahmananda Reddy personally, not the central government or Prime Minister Indira Gandhi — meaning the movement never developed a coherent anti-Centre political front.
*   Indira Gandhi eventually had Brahmananda Reddy resign in September 1971, replacing him with Telangana's own PV Narasimha Rao as Chief Minister; within a short time, the TPS merged into the Congress party, diluting the Telangana statehood aspiration.
*   The movement remained largely confined to **urban areas, district centres, and cities**, never spreading meaningfully to rural Telangana.
*   It was fought principally as an issue of jobs and surplus funds, without connecting to agriculture, on which most of Telangana's population depended — limiting its base of support.
*   In June 1969, the movement's top leaders were jailed, and the absence of an effective second line of leadership left the movement weakened thereafter.
*   National parties such as the Jana Sangh and the Communist parties supported a united state and opposed the separatist movement.
*   Chief Minister Brahmananda Reddy struck a deal with Congress-affiliated trade union leader Sanjeevayya, engineering the calling-off of the employees' indefinite strike.
*   Students became alienated from the movement once its leaders pressed them to resume classes and sit for exams rather than continue the boycott, prioritizing the academic year over the agitation.

**Lack of literature in the Movement:**

*   Another major reason the 1969 movement fell short of its goal was a lack of durable literature.
*   The movement was driven by aggressive slogans and provocative speeches, but lacked books systematically documenting the injustices, insults, and regional inequalities faced by Telangana people — weakening its capacity to build lasting, informed public support.

**Non-participation of the majority Muslim community:**

*   The majority Muslim community largely stayed out of the movement.
*   Kingshuk Nag (_Times of India_; Hyderabad resident), in his book _Telangana Movement – Historical Background_, attributes this to the aftermath of Partition-era violence: Razakars of the MIM party had carried out indiscriminate attacks on Hindus before Hyderabad state's merger into the Indian Union on 17 September, 1948.
*   After the merger, Hindus who resented the Razakars directed their anger at Muslims generally, which in turn made Muslims distrustful of Hindus and disinclined to join the 1969 movement.
*   These flaws were corrected only in the movement's later (second) phase.

**Results of the Movement:**

*   Despite its shortcomings, the movement produced effective future leadership for Telangana — for example, GM Anjaiah, active in 1969, later built huts for the homeless poor in Addagutta, Secunderabad.
*   Student leaders of 1969 — Jayashankar, Keshava Rao Jadhav, Bhupathi Krishnamurthy, and Kaloji Narayana Rao — went on to lead the movement's second phase.
*   A new culture of struggle spread among Telangana's people, which became instrumental in sustaining the later, second phase of the movement.

**Countering gendered attacks:** during the movement, hostility toward Andhra people extended into scandalous, insulting graffiti about women written on city walls; under Kumudin Naik's leadership, women organized to remove such writings from Himayat Nagar.

*   In May 1969, a women's conference was held at Hanumakonda presided over by Devaki, with Eswari Bhai as chief guest.
*   Freedom fighter Kanakaratnamma (MLC) led the women's movement in Warangal.

### Sangam Laxmibai (1911–1979)

*   Born in 1911 in a hamlet near Ghatkesar (Medchal district); educated at the University of Karve and Sharada Niketan (founded by Lakshmibayamma).
*   Played a role in the freedom movement, joining the Salt Satyagraha alongside Durga Bhai Deshmukh and imprisoned at Raivellur Jail until 1933; joined the anti-Simon Commission movement in 1928.
*   Elected to the Hyderabad State Legislature in 1952 from Banswada; served as Deputy Minister of Education in the Burgula government (1954–56).
*   Elected to the Lok Sabha from Medak on an Indian National Congress ticket in 1957, 1962, and 1967 — recognized as the **first woman elected to the Lok Sabha from Andhra Pradesh**.
*   During the 1969 movement, she prepared to resign her Medak MP seat.
*   Headed Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Movement in Telangana.
*   While in jail during the movement, she authored _Na Jailu Gnapakalu Anubhavalu_ ("My Prison Memories and Experiences").
*   Founded the **Indira Sevasadan Society**, aiding women and girls, and worked for women's welfare until her death in 1979.

### Masuma Begum

*   Born in 1901 in Hyderabad; awarded the Lady Baden Powell medal for her Indian Scout services.
*   Served as Minister of Social Welfare in the Damodaram Sanjeevaiah government while actively participating in the movement.
*   Recognized as the **first Muslim woman to hold ministerial office in India**.
*   Founded the _Anjuman-e-Kawathin_ organization, providing services to orphans; served as president of the All India Women's Conference (1962–64).
*   Supported the 1969 movement; awarded the **Padma Shri in 1974**.

### T.N. Sadalaxmi

*   Influenced colleagues with powerful speeches during the movement; her famous line — "If Telangana state comes, I will make it up as Bommarillu" — remains widely quoted.
*   Belonged to the Mehar caste, a Dalit sub-caste; recognized as the person who chaired the Telangana Praja Samithi.
*   Born in Bollaram, Hyderabad, in 1928; recognized as the **first Dalit woman legislator from Telangana**.
*   Initially elected from Peddapalli constituency, later from Kamareddy.
*   Served as Minister of Devadaya in Neelam Sanjivreddy's cabinet, and was the **first woman Deputy Speaker** during Damodaram Sanjeevaiah's tenure.
*   After a period with Congress, joined the Telugu Desam Party in 1982.
*   Founded the Bandhu Seva Mandali and the Leadcop organisation.

### J. Eshwaribai

*   Born in Secunderabad in 1918, into a common Dalit family; studied Ambedkar's theories and worked to further his aspirations.
*   Elected to the AP Legislative Assembly from Ellareddy constituency, Nizamabad district, on a Republican Party ticket.
*   Served as Republican Party secretary; became **National President of the Republican Party of India in 1986**.
*   In 1951, won as an Independent candidate from Chilakalaguda in the first-ever Hyderabad Municipal Corporation election.

### Kanakaratnamma

*   A member of the Legislature; led the Telangana movement in Warangal.

### Kumudini Nayak

*   Elected **Mayor of Hyderabad in 1962** — the **first woman Mayor of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation**.
*   Daughter of Pingali Venkata Rami Reddy, recognized as a Telangana torch-bearer (_vaitalikudu_).
*   Served as a member of the Legislative Assembly from Wanaparthy constituency, 1962–1972.

### Geetanjali Pillai and Hamsa Rani

*   On 6 August, 1969, under Kumari Geetanjali Pillai's leadership, twelve young women were arrested for satyagraha in Secunderabad.
*   Young women also performed satyagraha under Kumari Hamsa Rani's leadership at Chadar Ghat Bridge, Isamia Bazaar, and under Narasamma's leadership in Abids.

### Marri Chenna Reddy (1919–1996)

*   Born in Siripuram village, Vikarabad Taluk; initially worked as a doctor at Osmania Hospital before leaving the profession to join the national movement.
*   Organized the Telugu weekly magazine _Hyderabad_, run from Vijayawada.
*   A provisional member of Parliament from 1950–52; from 1952, a member of the Hyderabad Legislative Assembly, serving as Minister for Civil Supply, Agriculture, and Planning.
*   Elected to the AP State Legislative Assembly from Vikarabad in 1957; became a Lok Sabha member in 1967 and served as Union Minister of Mines & Minerals.
*   Elected **Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh on 6 March, 1978**; later served as Governor of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, and Tamil Nadu.
*   During his term as CM, **Ranga Reddy district was formed** (15 August, 1978), named after KV Ranga Reddy.
*   Became Chief Minister for a second time in 1989, resigning amid religious conflicts in Hyderabad's old city.

### KV Ranga Reddy (1890–1970)

*   Born in Pedda Mangalaram village, Chevella Taluk (now Rangareddy district).
*   Served as secretary of Reddy Hostel.
*   Established the _Vemanandhra Bhasha Nilayam_ at Nampally in 1923 with his own funds.
*   Presided over Andhra Mahasabha meetings at Shadnagar (1936) and Hyderabad (1943).
*   Founded AV College, Institute of Education, in 1944.
*   Served as Revenue Minister in the Burgula government (1952–56) and as **Andhra Pradesh's first Deputy Chief Minister** in Damodaram Sanjeevaiah's cabinet.
*   Authored _My Autobiography by KV Ranga Reddy_.
*   A member of the Indira Sevasadan Society founded by Sangam Lakshmibai in 1952.

### Makhdoom Mohiuddin (1908–1969)

*   Born in Andol, Medak district; a prominent Urdu revolutionary poet, titled _Shayar-e-Inquilab_ ("Poet of the Revolution").

**Literary works:**

*   _Piladushala_ (_Pasupu Pachcha Utariya_) — his earliest work, written as a student in 1932.
*   _Khoon ke Nakhoon_ — a play appreciated by Tagore.
*   The song "Jung hai Junge" and the poem "Bhagmathi," both popular nationwide.
*   _Bisat-e-Raqs_ — a compilation of poems and ghazals.
*   _Surk Savera_ ("The Red Dawn"), 1924.
*   _Gul-e-Taar_ ("The Dewdrenched Rose"), 1961.

**Famous ghazals**: _Ek chameli ki mandve taale_; _Aapki yaad aathi rahi raat bhar_; _Phir chide raat baat phoolonki_.

**Other biographical details:**

*   Awarded the **Sahitya Akademi Award in Urdu Literature in 1969**.
*   Participated in the Quit India Movement against British rule, and was a key figure in the movement seeking the Nizam's kingdom's merger into the Indian Union.
*   The seventh Nizam, believing his writings incited people against Hyderabad state, issued a _firman_ ordering his killing.
*   A founder of the Communist Party of Andhra Pradesh, and founder of the Comrade Association.
*   Met Yuri Gagarin, the first space traveller, during a visit to Russia, and wrote a poem about him.
*   His son, Nusrat Mohiuddin, served as secretary for Insaf Tehriq.

### JV Narsinga Rao

*   Joginapalli Venkata Narsinga Rao, born in Laksettipeta, Adilabad district.
*   Served as President of the Hyderabad PCC (1956) during the states' reorganization; elected to the legislature from Laksettipeta.

### Anantula Madan Mohan

*   Instrumental in establishing the TPS during the 1969 movement.
*   Won the Siddipet by-election on a TPS ticket in 1970, and was elected MLA from Siddipet in 1972, 1978, and 1983 (the seat was subsequently held by KCR, and, from 2004, by Harish Rao).
*   Served as the opposition leader for Congress when the Telugu Desam Party came to power in 1983.
*   JNTU was established during his tenure as Minister of Technical Education, Hyderabad.

### Tanguturi Anjaiah

*   Hometown: Banur village, Medak district.
*   Worked at the Alvin Metal Company in Hyderabad, rising to become a labour union leader.
*   Served as **Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh, 1980–82**; his unusually large cabinet was nicknamed the "Airbus cabinet."
*   Served as Central Labour Minister in 1984.
*   The first-ever World Telugu Conferences held abroad took place during his tenure as Chief Minister.

### Vandemataram Ramachandra Rao

*   Real name: Vavilala Ramachandra Rao.
*   Given the title "Vandemataram" by Veer Savarkar at a Pandaripuram meeting.
*   Authored the work _Hindu Sanghatan_.
*   Imprisoned in Bhagalpur jail, Bihar, for participating in the Quit India Movement.

*   Sridhar Reddy resolved to erect a monument commemorating the martyrs of the 1969 separate-Telangana movement.
*   City Mayor S. Lakshminarayana laid the memorial's foundation stone on **23 February, 1970**, at Gun Park (opposite the Assembly), despite several legal injunctions against doing so.
*   The night before the foundation ceremony, Pratap Kishore and Williams Anthi gathered martyrs' personal belongings — books, certificates, and similar items — and placed them at the memorial's base.
*   Leaders arrested for attending the foundation ceremony included Manik Rao, Chenna Reddy, E.V. Padmanabhan, T. Anjaiah, T. Govind Singh, and MM Hashim.
*   The stupa itself was carved by **Ekka Yadagiri Rao**, and was completed in 1975.
*   City Deputy Mayor M. Ramachandraiah inaugurated the memorial on **25 February, 1970**, at the Clock Tower area, Secunderabad.

**Symbolism of the memorial's design:**

*   The stupa's base is made of black stone, with nine holes on each of its four sides bearing inscriptions — the nine holes symbolizing the nine districts of the then-Telangana region.
*   Above the base rises a stupa of red stone; red was chosen to symbolize sacrifice.
*   An Ashoka Chakra sits atop the stupa; this Dharma Chakra signifies that the movement's martyrs sacrificed their lives in defence of Dharma (truth).
*   At the stupa's centre is a _makara thoranam_, an architectural motif drawn from the Sanchi Stupa.
*   The stupa's vertical portion bears nine white stone flowers (nine-petalled jasmine blooms), symbolizing both sacrifice and peace.

### Fragmented Telangana Political Leadership

*   Telangana lacked a single leader broadly acceptable across the whole state, a gap that persisted through the Brahmananda Reddy years.
*   Under the Gentlemen's Agreement, if the Chief Minister came from Andhra, the Deputy Chief Minister's post was meant to go to Telangana — but the arrangement was applied unevenly: Sanjeevareddy, for instance, held the Deputy CM post only briefly before it changed hands.
*   By 1967, when Brahmananda Reddy became Chief Minister, many shortcomings in implementing the Gentlemen's Agreement had already surfaced, and the regional committee meant to safeguard Telangana had become largely nominal in practice.
*   After Achyutha Reddy's tenure as committee chairman, Telangana's political representation splintered between rival camps — one under Achyutha Reddy, another under Hayagriva Chari — undermining a unified Telangana political voice even as the movement gathered pace.

### The Unresolved Seniority List Issue

*   Even 15 years after Andhra Pradesh's formation, a joint seniority list combining employees of both regions had still not been finalized.
*   Inequities and irregularities in the interim arrangements were regularly pointed out by Telangana employees, while a recurring core grievance was that Telangana's funds were being diverted to Andhra rather than spent within the region — a complaint that ran throughout the movement's employee-related demands.
*   Telangana government employees in particular grew increasingly restive over this unresolved status, feeding into the broader employee unrest already detailed under "Dissatisfaction Among Employees" above.

### The All-Party Committee — Central Government Oversight Mechanism

*   As part of the All-Party Agreement's implementation, two senior officials were designated to ensure the removal of non-natives from posts reserved for Telangana locals was carried out properly, and that no compensation was paid for such displacement beyond what the agreement specified.
*   Under the arrangement, if suitable Telangana natives were unavailable for a reserved post, the post was to be kept vacant rather than filled by a non-native, and departments were instructed not to allow local reservation requirements to be circumvented through administrative loopholes.
*   Non-native employees removed under this process were to be given employment opportunities in the Andhra region without loss of service benefits, with additional posts created there if necessary.

### Seniority List Preparation Rules

*   The rules specified that a single seniority list should be prepared for Andhra and Telangana employees together, based on their designated posts, applying uniformly wherever the Central Government had approved a list, or, where no such approved list existed, applying whatever provisional list the state government was currently following — while committing that no adverse action would be taken against employees on the basis of any list not yet approved by the Centre.

### The Question of Telangana's Surplus Funds — Broader Political Context

*   The all-party agreement's discussions on surplus funds proceeded alongside efforts to dispel misconceptions about how much of Telangana's revenue had genuinely gone unspent within the region; this is the same subject examined in detail by the Kumar Lalith and Bhargava Committees (see the earlier section on these committees), which put the unspent surplus at **Rs 34.10 crore** and **Rs 28.34 crore** respectively.
*   After the 1956 Gentlemen's Agreement, a further arrangement more favourable to Telangana was reached as the movement intensified, though some of the officials responsible for implementing it were themselves implicated in irregularities as the agitation deepened.
*   To address the risk of 4,500 identified non-mulki employees in Telangana being difficult to relocate to Andhra given Supreme Court constraints, the Chief Minister created **2,000 new posts specifically for Telangana** and empowered Collectors to fill them locally.

### The Vanchu (Wanchoo) Committee — Additional Detail on Its Constitutional Reasoning

*   A committee headed by former Supreme Court Chief Justice K.N. Wanchoo, with Central Government Attorney General M.C. Setalvad and former Attorney General Niren De as members, was tasked with finding constitutionally sound ways to protect Mulki-based employment safeguards.
*   The committee's central finding was that, while the Constitution empowers Parliament to legislate residency-based preferences for an entire state's employment, it does not empower Parliament to restrict such preference to only one region within a state — meaning continued Mulki Rules of the kind Telangana sought were constitutionally unsustainable in their original form (this corroborates and adds constitutional reasoning to the Wanchoo Committee findings already detailed in the earlier section).
*   The Committee accordingly held that no law could guarantee this kind of protection to any one district, taluka, or village's residents in a way that fully insulated local job access from the wider state's workforce — a structural limitation the Vanchu Committee itself flagged as the reason it recommended devolving administrative hiring authority (over Class III and IV posts) to the Telangana Regional Committee and local Collectors instead of relying on residency law.

### Nagarjuna Sagar and Canal-Water Diversion Grievance

*   When Hyderabad's engineers originally designed the Nagarjuna Sagar project, the plan was for its left-canal waters to irrigate land beginning around Guntur district and extending across parts of coastal Andhra, while some portion of the canal was also meant to irrigate land in Telangana's Nalgonda, Khammam, and Warangal districts along the Musi/Krishna–Godavari belt.
*   Under the scheme, water was meant to reach the Nandigama area via Distributory 19, requiring canal construction to reach Nandigama; however, before that canal construction was completed, water from Distributory 16 was diverted directly to the Nandigama region — bypassing the planned sequence and effectively earmarking the area's water supply ahead of schedule.
*   This came to be seen, in Telangana public perception, as evidence that irrigation infrastructure nominally classified as a shared "K.L. Project" was, in practice, being used to prioritize Andhra-region needs over Telangana's, deepening the region's sense of economic marginalization already reflected in the Pochampad-funding grievance described earlier under "9 January — Warangal Meeting."

### Other Reasons for the Agitation

*   Telangana and Andhra employees did not get along well at a basic working level: Andhra employees, considering themselves more knowledgeable, tended to look down on their Telangana counterparts.
*   Telangana employees generally worked at a steady, unhurried pace, while Andhra employees worked with greater urgency and speed when performing tasks — a difference in working style that made it difficult for each side to understand the other and fostered mutual suspicion and envy.
*   Telangana officials, regardless of whether they were Hindu or Muslim, tended to treat people evenhandedly in work-related matters, whereas the conduct of Andhra government employees was perceived as noticeably different in this respect — a perceived double standard that increased mistrust between the two communities' officials.
*   Andhra cultivators began purchasing Telangana farmers' land at low prices (roughly three to five hundred rupees per acre) and then raising crop yields dramatically on that same land — since Telangana farmers who sold their land often ended up needing to work as labourers on their own former fields. 

*   Because migrant Andhra farmers demanded far less in wages than local Telangana labour required, this caused deep psychological distress in Telangana's rural communities. This land-alienation dimension never received serious attention from the region's political associations at the time, since — as the saying goes, "whoever needs the sale has less bargaining power" — those forced to sell were rarely in a position to hold out for a fair price.
